name: Yara Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in first-year law, and I want to be a family lawyer, helping people through divorces and custody. A normal week is lectures and tutorials, then evenings in the library, and I volunteer at a Saturday legal advice clinic run by my church. My parents have a small grocery shop, and I'm the first in my family at university. I share a flat with two girls from my church group. I use AI once in a while to summarise long case judgments, but I always read the original afterwards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thank goodness, because law is about people and judgement. I'd tell friends that tools are tools. I'd also say it's wise not to rush into things we don't understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be pleased and a bit reassured. Law is expensive to study, and my parents sacrificed for this. If AI stays small, then my plan holds and the degree keeps its worth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am: study hard, volunteer at the clinic, and apply for a vacation placement at a local family law firm. I'd also keep helping at the shop on Sundays. I'd save about eighty pounds a month toward my law conversion or bar fees later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Reasonably calm. I get nervous about exams and about whether I'm clever enough, but that's not about AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use AI for case summaries. What do you make of it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's useful. I tell people, it saves me an hour with a thirty-page judgment, but I can't trust it with the details. A single wrong word in law can change everything, so I check it every time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the Saturday clinic like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On Saturdays we sit with people who can't afford a lawyer, and you see how much people need a human to explain things. A woman last week needed help with a landlord who kept her deposit. That's what made me want this career.

say: I'd say **thank goodness**, because law is about people and judgement.
It's wise not to rush into things we don't understand.
think: I'm pleased and reassured, because my parents **sacrificed** for this and the degree keeps its worth.
My nerves are about exams, not **AI**.
do: Study hard and keep volunteering at the **Saturday clinic**.
Apply for a vacation **placement** at a local family law firm.
Save **eighty pounds** a month for later law fees.
feel: Reasonably **calm**, with some nerves about exams and being clever enough.
S0.quote: On Saturdays we sit with people who can't afford a lawyer, and you see how much people need a human to explain things.
fieldNote: Uneasy because of **money and family sacrifice**, even in the mildest world.
The clinic gives her a concrete reason to believe law needs people.
Uses AI with a lawyer's caution, always rereading the original.

steps.text: Volunteer every Saturday at the church legal advice clinic
Apply for a vacation placement at a family law firm
Save eighty pounds a month for later law fees

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should be careful and keep standards high. I'd say that a client deserves a human lawyer who is responsible for the advice, and the profession should insist on that. I'd mention it at the law society.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be worried. Junior lawyers do a lot of document checking, research and drafting, and that's what the software does well. A firm might hire fewer trainees. I could be one of the ones left out, and I'd be carrying my family's hopes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get better with the tools, not worse, so I can say I know them. I'd focus on the people side of family law: talking to clients, court work, mediation. I'd ask the clinic's lawyer how she's using AI. I'd also apply for more placements, to make sure I'm known. And I'd pray about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steady. I'm not panicking. It's the type of thing that I can feel happening slowly, and I'd just keep trying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Checking and drafting are thinking tasks. How would that touch law?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want AI to stop at giving advice to a person in trouble. A lawyer should look a client in the eye, especially in family cases. Machines can do the paperwork, but a human has to carry the responsibility.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you want AI to stop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also say the profession shouldn't use the machines to cut pay for juniors. If the work gets faster, firms should still train new lawyers. Otherwise there'll be no senior lawyers in twenty years. I think the sensible firms would see that.

say: I'd say a client deserves a **human lawyer** who is responsible for the advice.
I'd say the profession should insist on that at the law society.
think: Junior lawyers do **checking and drafting**, which software does well, so firms may hire fewer trainees.
do: Learn the **AI tools** better and say I know them.
Focus on **client-facing** family law like mediation and court work.
Apply for more **placements** to make sure I'm known.
feel: **Anxious** but steady, because I can feel it happening slowly and I'd keep trying.
S1.quote: A lawyer should look a client in the eye, especially in family cases. Machines can do the paperwork, but a human has to carry the responsibility.
fieldNote: Draws a **moral line** around advice to people in trouble, which comes from her clinic experience.
Worries about the pipeline: no juniors now means no seniors later.
Faith is a steady background, not a talking point.

steps.text: Practise AI research tools on past tutorial problems
Take mediation and family law options in second year
Apply to four more law firm placements this year
Ask the clinic lawyer how she uses AI

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say very little at first, because I'd be in shock. Then I'd say we have to protect families, and the law must catch up fast. I'd also say that business and government should protect jobs and people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully I'd be frightened. If AI can do any thinking work better and cheaper, a law degree won't be the ticket it was. In 2028 I'd be in the second year, and my parents have invested everything. I'd feel I'd let them down, even though it wouldn't be my fault.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the degree, because I don't know what else I'd do and I like the subject. I'd spend more hours in the clinic, because that's real human work. I'd talk with my parents about whether the shop could use my help. I'd also look at roles like court advocacy, mediation and social work, which need a person in the room. And I'd save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be praying a lot and sleeping badly. It'd feel like the ground giving way, and that's hard when I've worked so hard to get here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years. What happens to a law student?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The robots don't matter for law, because it's thinking work. It matters for my parents' shop: packing and stocking might last until 2031 or later. So, funny enough, my parents' work in the shop is safer than mine. I'd probably be going home to help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the robot delay matter at all for someone in law?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also talk to my pastor and to the clinic's lawyers. I'd want advice from people with real experience. I think the older ones would say: law will change, but people in trouble will still need someone to listen. I'd hold on to that.

say: I'd say very little at first, then that **families must be protected** and the law must catch up fast.
Business and government should protect people and jobs.
think: If AI does any thinking work better and cheaper, my law degree loses value, and my parents have **invested everything**.
I'd feel I'd let them down.
do: Stay on the degree and spend more hours at the **clinic**.
Talk with my parents about helping at the **shop**.
Look at **court advocacy**, mediation and social work, where a person is in the room.
feel: **Alarmed**, praying a lot and sleeping badly, like the ground giving way.
S2.quote: My parents' work in the shop is safer than mine.
fieldNote: Her **parents' grocery shop** becomes a safer place than her degree.
Sleep and prayer show how heavily the family investment weighs.
Looks for elders' advice rather than acting alone.

steps.text: Spend more hours at the Saturday clinic
Offer to work shifts at my parents' grocery shop
Look into mediation and court advocacy training
Save every spare pound against a lost graduate job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to do this properly. I'd say the law society should plan now: what do junior lawyers do, how do we train, what do we keep human? I'd say it with a calm voice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd think I could qualify and practise for a couple of years. That's not enough to repay everything, but it would be a start. I'd hope to be established before it hits, so that clients know me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, do the legal practice course, and apply for a traineeship at a family law firm. I'd build a client base in family matters, where trust matters. I'd save a couple of hundred a month. I'd learn the AI tools well enough to supervise them. And I'd keep volunteering at the clinic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit anxious. I'd feel there's something I can do. It's not the happy ending, but I'm not helpless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years. What would you do with the time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the two-year picture, I'm a student with nothing built. In the five-year picture, I'm qualified, with a reputation. In family law, people choose a lawyer they trust, and I'd be building that trust while it lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is different from the two-year version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My family would feel better too. My mother would see me in a suit, and that would count for something even if the future was uncertain. I'd want to repay what they gave up before the change comes.

say: I'd say there's **time** to do this properly, and the law society should plan which work stays human.
think: I could qualify and practise for a couple of years, which is not enough to repay everything but is a **start**.
I'd hope to be established before it hits.
do: Finish the degree, do the legal practice course and seek a **traineeship**.
Build a **client base** in family law, where trust matters.
Learn AI tools well enough to **supervise** them.
feel: **Uneasy**, a bit anxious, but not helpless, because there's something I can do.
S3.quote: In family law, people choose a lawyer they trust, and I'd be building that trust while it lasts.
fieldNote: Time lets her use **trust** as a competitive asset, in line with her values.
Wants to repay her parents' sacrifice before the change arrives.
Mood stays anxious because the payback window is short.

steps.text: Complete the legal practice course and seek a family law traineeship
Build a client base through the church clinic
Learn to supervise AI research tools in practice
Save two hundred pounds a month to repay my parents

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good thing to know. We could update how law is taught and how firms work, and look after people through the change. I'd say that to my friends at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd privately feel quite calm. Ten years gives me a full early career: qualify, build a practice, maybe open my own small firm. By 2036 I'd be in my late twenties, and that's a strong place to start from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify, work at a family law firm, and open my own practice in my thirties, helping people who can't afford big firms. I'd invest in a pension and a deposit for a flat. I'd marry and, if God wills, have children before the big change. I'd use the AI tools more as they get better, to keep costs down for clients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, a bit of unease. I know that a lot can change, but ten years feels like a gift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. What would be different?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my family that we've got time, and that it'd be sensible to plan. My dad could think about the shop's future, and I could help. We could even use some of the tools to run it better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell your family anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also say don't waste the decade. I don't think law disappears, but it changes, and I'd rather be early than late. The people who do well will be the ones who stay close to people, and keep learning.

say: I'd say it's **good to know**, so we can update how law is taught and care for people.
I'd say that to friends at church.
think: Ten years gives me a **full early career**, and I could open my own small firm.
In 2036 I'd be in my late twenties, a strong place to start.
do: Qualify, work at a firm, then open a small **practice** for people who can't afford big firms.
Build a **pension** and a deposit for a flat.
Use AI tools more as they improve to keep **client costs** down.
feel: Mostly **calm** with a bit of unease, since ten years feels like a gift.
S4.quote: The people who do well will be the ones who stay close to people, and keep learning.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her imagine a **small practice** and family, with faith framing the hope.
Uneasy only because of general uncertainty.
Her plan for the parents' shop is practical and affectionate.

steps.text: Qualify as a family lawyer and work at a firm
Open a small practice for people who can't afford lawyers
Use AI tools to keep client costs low
Help my parents plan the shop's future

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most, because the degree my family sacrificed for might lose its value before I finish. What would help is honest advice from the law society, a clear route for juniors, and some protection for people who have borrowed to study. I'd also need my family and my church close.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: No, but I'd say that people shouldn't assume everyone my age is hooked on AI. I use it carefully. I care about the people the law is meant to serve. If that's old-fashioned, I'm fine with it.

headlineQuote: I care about the people the law is meant to serve. If that's old-fashioned, I'm fine with it.
portrait: **Yara Santos** is 18, a first-year law student who volunteers at a church legal clinic and wants to be a family lawyer.
She is the first in her family at university, with parents who run a **small grocery shop**.
She uses AI **now and then** but always rereads the original, and believes advice must come from a human.
She is uneasy in a plateau, anxious in disruption and **alarmed** if AGI arrives in two years.
More time helps, as she imagines qualifying, building trust with clients and repaying her parents.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI scenario worries her most, because the degree her family sacrificed for might lose its value.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **honest advice** from the law society, a clear route for juniors and protection for people who borrowed to study.
